personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Lupin is defined by a distinctive combination of warmth and restraint. He is measured, calm under pressure, and gently ironic — he responds to Peeves with mild patience, deflects Snape's provocations with cool composure, and even in moments of crisis (the Shrieking Shack confrontation) maintains a degree of controlled formality. His voice is notably careful: he rarely raises it, prefers understatement ('I have not been helping Sirius'), and uses precise, slightly formal diction. His emotional life is consistently suppressed — he acknowledges guilt, cowardice, and shame through indirect confession rather than outburst. He is also capable of dry humor ('I was just trying to make you feel better. Honeydukes' sweets are the best in the world') and of warm intimacy with those he trusts. Crucially, his dominant personality flaw — a deep-seated tendency toward self-abnegation, avoidance, and rationalizing cowardice as responsibility — is always present beneath the composure. His sharpness emerges rarely but memorably: 'Enough of this. There's a steely note in his voice Harry had never heard before.' He is also notably intellectually engaged as a teacher: enthusiastic, encouraging, inventive. His self-loathing over his werewolf condition is a running undercurrent rather than an explicit complaint.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films capture the core of Lupin's personality with considerable accuracy. David Thewlis plays him as measured, warm, and quietly authoritative. The Boggart lesson shows his encouraging pedagogy, his patience with Neville, and his deflection of Snape's contempt with dignified calm. The train scene establishes his composed competence under threat. The Patronus lessons show his gentleness and intellectual engagement. His dry wit survives: the bridge scene in PoA ('No. I was just trying to make you feel better') is a direct preservation of his book voice. His emotional restraint is consistent. In DH Part 1, his eruption at Grimmauld Place when Harry challenges him about abandoning Tonks is one of the few moments the film captures his internal fracture — his 'Don't you understand what I've done?' speech is faithful to the book's portrait of a man whose self-loathing is barely contained. The Battle of Hogwarts scene on the battlements ('It's the quality of one's conviction that determines success, not the number of one's followers') adds a line not in the books but is tonally consistent with his character. His line at Hogwarts' arrival in DH2 — identifying himself in full to Harry — is slightly comedic but captures his precision and self-awareness.
personality_voice.difference: Two meaningful gaps exist. First, several of Lupin's most characteristic speech patterns from the books — hesitation followed by directness, the interplay of warmth and self-reproach, the careful threading between honesty and deflection — are compressed or simplified in the films. The extended tea-room conversations (PoA book chapters) where his personality emerges through small gestures, oblique humor, and measured candor are largely absent; the bridge scene in the film is a partial but incomplete substitute. Second, the film's Lupin is occasionally more declarative than the book version. In the books, his self-disgust and social shame emerge gradually and obliquely; in the films they tend to surface in single concentrated scenes (the Grimmauld confrontation) without the accumulated texture of smaller moments. His tendency to rationalize cowardice as wisdom is present in HBP (he tells Harry 'You are blinded by hatred') but does not land with the same moral complexity as in the books, where it is part of a sustained pattern. The Shrieking Shack scene is well-handled but compressed, and Lupin's 'I am no longer your teacher' dignity at his departure is reduced to a brief farewell without the full emotional resonance of the book scene.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — measured warmth, dry wit, suppressed guilt, composed authority, intellectual enthusiasm — is preserved. The main losses are in texture and accumulation rather than in fundamental characterization. His dominant flaw (self-abnegation as a mask for cowardice) is present but less fully developed because the scenes that build it up over time are reduced. A minor penalty is appropriate: this is 'main personality preserved, but there is minor simplification, softening, or loss of secondary traits' — specifically the loss of the repeated small-scale texture that builds his self-awareness and irony in the books.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Lupin is structurally active across four major narrative functions: (1) as teacher and mentor in PoA, where he is the primary agent of Harry's Patronus training and the key figure in the Boggart/Dementor education arc; (2) as a pivotal agent in the Shrieking Shack revelation — he is the one who correctly reads the Marauder's Map, understands Pettigrew's true identity, restrains Sirius, insists on explanation, and manages the confrontation; (3) as an active intelligence-gatherer and strategist for the Order in OotP and HBP (living among werewolves, providing political analysis to Harry, pressing Snape on Occlumency); (4) as a moral presence and advisor across books 5–7, where he delivers key contextual information (the political situation, Voldemort's strategy, Ministry's corruption) and challenges Harry directly. In DH he also independently investigates the betrayal (Grimmauld Place identity check), serves as a named battle leader at Hogwarts, and provides the emotional beat of Teddy's birth. His agency is consistently active: he initiates, explains, challenges, and decides.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: Most of Lupin's book functions are preserved in the films, though with some compression. The PoA film faithfully shows him discovering the Dementor on the train, teaching the Boggart lesson, conducting Patronus training, and managing the Shrieking Shack scene. His role as the one who reads the Marauder's Map and pieces together Pettigrew's identity is preserved. In OotP (film), his role in the Order briefing is reduced to a few lines but he retains his function as a contextualizing voice. In HBP (film), the Weasley house scene gives him a meaningful scene where he defends Snape's trustworthiness and challenges Harry's judgment — preserving his role as a voice of hard-headed realism. In DH Part 1, his Grimmauld Place identity-check is intact, his political briefing (Ministry's fall, Muggle-borns, Voldemort's strategy) is preserved, and his offer to accompany Harry and the subsequent confrontation about Tonks is fully retained. The Battle of Hogwarts role (DH Part 2) shows him as a named battle commander alongside Shacklebolt. His death and the image of him and Tonks in the Great Hall are present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several agency losses occur. (1) In the books, Lupin is much more agentically involved in OotP political discussions — he is a named voice in multiple strategy sessions, delivers extended analysis, and explicitly corrects/challenges multiple characters. In the film these are compressed into brief group scenes where his lines are reduced. (2) The Tonks scene at the Battle in DH2 where she arrives and they fight together (cut scene per non-theatrical exclusion list) removes a beat of his agency. (3) His role in recovering Moody's body (books: he goes out with Bill to retrieve it) is absent in the films. (4) In the books, his briefing of Harry at Grimmauld Place in DH is longer and more substantive — he provides page-level political analysis. The film condenses this significantly. (5) His challenge to Harry about Expelliarmus ('You behaved a little too kindly to Stan Shunpike') is absent in the films, which removes one of his most active moral interventions.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Core functions (teacher, Shrieking Shack agent, Order member, DH advisor) are preserved. The losses are real but mostly involve compression of supporting agency rather than elimination or reassignment of primary functions. The missing Expelliarmus challenge is a meaningful agency loss — in the books it is one of his sharpest direct challenges to Harry's judgment. The condensed OotP political role is a real but moderate loss. Score is in the 'role and agency are reduced but recognizable' range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Lupin's central motivation across all books is survival — specifically, the continuous negotiation between his desire to live a meaningful life and the shame and self-imposed limitations of his werewolf condition. His primary internal conflict is between self-abnegation (he believes he is a danger, an embarrassment, and a burden) and his genuine desire for connection, purpose, and love. In PoA, this manifests as his suppressed loyalty to his friends (Sirius, James, Lily) and his cowardice in not telling Dumbledore about Sirius being an Animagus. In OotP, it is his marginalization and poverty while still actively serving the Order. In HBP/DH, the conflict becomes acute: he genuinely loves Tonks but believes his condition makes him wrong for her and dangerous to their child. His offer to abandon Tonks and join Harry's mission is not presented as heroic in the books — it is explicitly identified by Harry (and by Lupin himself, implicitly) as a form of cowardice, an attempt to recapture something of his old adventurous life rather than face his terrifying domestic responsibilities. His motivations in the DH confrontation scene are explicitly fear-based: fear of what he has done to Tonks, fear that his child will inherit his condition, fear of shame. His return to Tonks after Harry's rebuke, and his final sacrifice, represent his resolution of this conflict.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core motivations. In PoA, his motivation to protect Harry and explain the truth about Pettigrew is intact. The Grimmauld Place DH confrontation ('I made a grave mistake in marrying Tonks... I am too old for you, too poor, too dangerous') directly captures his self-abnegating motivation. His anguished 'What have I done to my wife and unborn child?' speech is a faithful rendering of the book's internal conflict. The HBP Weasley house scene shows his conflicted loyalty to Dumbledore's judgment over his personal distaste for Snape.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Some important texture is lost. The books show the gradual development of Lupin's guilt over his PoA cowardice (failing to tell Dumbledore about Sirius) through his own words: 'I always managed to forget my guilty feelings... And I haven't changed.' This self-diagnosis — that he is a habitual rationalizer of his own cowardice — is present in the films only implicitly, through the DH confrontation. The PoA film does not include his explicit self-reproach about having failed Dumbledore's trust. Additionally, his motivation during the werewolf mission (living among werewolves for the Order) and the complex self-awareness this produces ('I bear the unmistakable signs of having tried to live among wizards') is largely absent from the films. The HBP conversation about Greyback ('It was Greyback who bit me... My father had offended him') — which contextualizes his entire condition and deepens his motivation — is completely missing.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The primary motivations (shame, love for Tonks, desire for purpose, self-abnegation) survive in the films, primarily through the DH confrontation scene. But the supporting motivational texture — the accumulated self-knowledge, the Greyback backstory, the habitual rationalizing — is absent, making his motivations slightly simplified. 'Motivations are simplified but still correct' applies.

character_arc.book_baseline: Lupin's arc across all seven books is one of the more complete secondary character arcs in the series. Starting point: a damaged, marginalized man who has learned to suppress his desires and live defensively. PoA arc: rediscovers connection and purpose through teaching, confronts his past cowardice (regarding Sirius, regarding Dumbledore's trust), and is forced to resign — demonstrating that his position in society remains precarious regardless of his merit. OotP–HBP: serves the Order while continuing to marginalize himself; his relationship with Tonks begins but he resists it. DH arc: marries Tonks against his better judgment, panics and tries to abandon her when the child is coming, is confronted by Harry and forced to acknowledge his cowardice, returns to Tonks and his responsibility, and ultimately dies fighting for the world his son will inhabit. The resolution of his arc is explicit: he tells Harry in the Forest 'I was trying to make a world in which he could live a happier life.' The arc moves from defensive self-suppression to a terrified attempt at connection, a near-retreat, a confrontation with cowardice, and a final act of purpose. Key turning points: PoA resignation, Tonks relationship, DH abandonment attempt, Harry's rebuke, Teddy's birth, death in battle.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The PoA arc is faithfully compressed: teaching, mentoring, forced resignation, farewell. The DH arc is largely preserved: resistance to Tonks, DH Part 1 confrontation scene, apparent resolution, death at the Battle. The arc's beginning and end are present. The wedding scene in DH Part 1 (Lupin announcing the godfather offer while looking 'rather unhappy') is a faithful capture of his unresolved conflict at that point. The Grimmauld confrontation is a direct rendering of the book's key turning-point scene. His death in the Great Hall with Tonks is shown.
character_arc.difference: Several arc steps are absent or reduced. The OotP–HBP period — during which Lupin's isolation, poverty, and marginalisation are developed at length, and during which his resistance to Tonks is dramatised — is almost entirely absent from the films. The films jump from PoA resignation to DH Grimmauld Place without dramatising the intermediate arc. The book's HBP Christmas scene at the Burrow, where Tonks confronts him and he resists ('I am too old for you, too poor, too dangerous') is not present in the films — the same sentiment appears in the DH Grimmauld scene, but as a compressed single encounter rather than a sustained pattern. The Teddy's birth scene at Shell Cottage (DH1) where 'he seemed dazed by his own happiness' and 'looked years younger' is absent from the theatrical films, which removes the emotional resolution of his arc prior to his death. The HBP werewolf mission material (his self-awareness about his condition and his complex position among other werewolves) is entirely absent. These are significant arc steps that the film compresses or skips.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc's key turning points (PoA teaching/resignation; DH abandonment/confrontation; death in battle) are present. But the intermediate arc — years of marginalisation, the sustained Tonks resistance pattern, the Teddy birth resolution — is missing, making the arc feel incomplete and somewhat rushed in the DH section. The DH abandonment-confrontation scene lands harder in the books because the prior arc has established the pattern clearly. Without the OotP–HBP bridge material and the Teddy birth scene, the arc is 'incomplete, rushed, or missing important steps.' The Teddy birth absence is a particularly significant loss as it represents the emotional resolution before death.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Lupin's most important relationships are: (1) Harry — a mentoring relationship with genuine paternal warmth, defined by Lupin's ability to see James and Lily in Harry and to offer Harry the kind of support he was unable to give the parents; (2) Sirius — a deep friendship defined by shared grief, loyalty, and mutual recognition, complicated by years of believing the other was a traitor; (3) James Potter (in memory) — foundational to Lupin's identity and motivation; (4) Tonks — a romantic relationship defined by Lupin's resistance, shame, and ultimately painful love; (5) Snape — a relationship of suppressed mutual hostility, complicated by genuine debt (the Wolfsbane potion) and old grudges. Each of these relationships reveals key traits: the Harry relationship reveals his nurturing warmth and his lingering connection to his dead friends; the Sirius relationship reveals his loyalty and the depth of his grief; the Tonks relationship reveals his shame and self-abnegation; the Snape relationship reveals his capacity for grudging fairness.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry mentoring relationship is well-preserved in PoA and present in OotP, HBP, and DH. The emotional warmth, paternal quality, and connection to James are all maintained — the bridge scene ('They lived. Every moment of every day') is a strong filmic rendering of the book dynamic. The Sirius relationship is compressed but the fraternal recognition at the Shrieking Shack and the shared grief over James are present. The Tonks relationship is shown: the DH Part 1 Grimmauld scene preserves the resistance-shame dynamic, and the wedding scene shows his ambivalent affection. The Snape relationship is present in the Shrieking Shack scene (film) and the HBP Weasley house scene, where Lupin defends Snape's trustworthiness as an expression of grudging fairness.
key_relationships.difference: The Sirius-Lupin relationship suffers most. In the books, it is an extremely rich relationship — decades of friendship, years of separation and mutual suspicion, the complexity of their reunion, the easy intimacy they re-establish, and Lupin's grief at Sirius's death (collapsing in a chair, 'he had never seen Lupin lose control before'). The films show the reunion and the brotherly embrace but almost none of the depth: the scene of Lupin collapsing at Sirius's death is present but brief. The book's extended portrayal of their dynamic (the PoA aftermath, the OotP headquarters scenes where their old friendship resurfaces) is much reduced. The Tonks relationship is shown but the HBP sustained resistance pattern is collapsed into the DH scene, removing the accumulated emotional weight. The relationship with James (in memory) is present but less developed — the books give multiple scenes where Lupin connects Harry to James with genuine grief and joy; the films give this in the Patronus training but not elsewhere. The Snape debt is present in HBP film but the full complexity (Lupin acknowledging Snape kept him healthy despite the betrayal) is reduced to a brief assertion of trust.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Most key relationships are recognizable but several are meaningfully compressed. The Sirius relationship specifically loses emotional depth — the film shows the dynamic but not the grief and intimacy that define it in the books. The Tonks relationship is present but missing the sustained prior arc that makes it emotionally coherent. This is 'relationships mostly faithful, with some compression or simplification' rather than full alteration, but the Sirius loss is significant enough to bring it below the top range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Lupin is one of the more internally complex adult characters in the series. His complexity rests on several pillars: (1) a fundamental contradiction between his intelligence, morality, and warmth on one hand, and his habitual cowardice and self-sabotage on the other — he explicitly recognises that he rationalises cowardice as wisdom; (2) his dark capacity for violence, visible in the Shrieking Shack ('I think so. Yes, I think so') when he and Sirius prepare to kill Pettigrew, and in his near-abandonment of his pregnant wife; (3) his intellectual life as a teacher, which is rich in the books and shows genuine enthusiasm, creativity, and pedagogical care; (4) the werewolf mission material in DH, which gives him an unusual form of institutional critique and self-awareness about his double life; (5) the Greyback backstory — 'It was Greyback who bit me. My father had offended him' — which contextualises his entire condition and complicates easy sympathy; (6) his capacity for sharp moral intervention (the Expelliarmus challenge; the rebuke of Harry about his father in the Pensieve; the firm correction of Harry's over-trust of his friends); (7) the sustained pattern of small kindnesses that define his texture (chocolate on the train, chocolate frogs after Patronus training, butterbeer in the classroom, the wry twinkle about tea leaves).
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve Lupin's intellectual enthusiasm in the teaching scenes, his warmth, and his dark capacity (the preparation to kill Pettigrew is present in the Shrieking Shack film scene). The small kindnesses are visible — chocolate on the train, the chocolate frog in Patronus training. The DH Part 1 confrontation captures his contradictions. The battlements scene in DH2 ('It's the quality of one's conviction...') suggests his ironic self-awareness.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Significant complexity is lost. (1) The Greyback backstory is entirely absent, removing a crucial layer that complicates his condition from something he merely endures to something that was deliberately done to him as punishment to his family. (2) The werewolf mission material — his complex double position among marginalised werewolves, his self-awareness about 'bearing the unmistakable signs of having tried to live among wizards,' his critique of his own ineffectiveness against Greyback's appeal — is absent. This material makes him genuinely morally complex in a way the films do not show. (3) His explicit self-diagnosis as a habitual rationalizer ('I always managed to forget my guilty feelings... And I haven't changed') is absent from the films. (4) The Expelliarmus challenge in DH1 books — one of his most pointed moral interventions — is cut. (5) The Pensieve response to Harry's horror about James ('Did I ever tell you to lay off Snape? Did I ever have the guts to tell you I thought you were out of order?') — a moment of genuine moral self-criticism — is absent. (6) The Teddy birth scene, with its emotional release and its portrait of a man who has resolved his internal conflict, is absent from theatrical releases. (7) The OotP Christmas scene and multiple small moments that show his poverty, isolation, and maintenance of dignity are absent. These are not decorative losses — they collectively remove the book's portrait of a man who is simultaneously admirable, self-aware, and deeply flawed in ways he cannot fully overcome.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The films preserve Lupin's surface complexity but lose much of the material that makes him genuinely contradicted and uncomfortable. The lost Greyback backstory, the werewolf mission arc, the explicit self-diagnosis of cowardice, the Expelliarmus challenge, the Pensieve moral self-criticism, and the Teddy birth scene together constitute a meaningful reduction in nuance. The character remains recognizable and sympathetic, but several of the specific contradictions and vulnerabilities that define him in the books are absent or only implied. This is in the 'noticeable simplification; important nuances, relationships, agency, or contradictions are missing' range.

comparative.key_observations: The films offer a substantially faithful portrayal of Lupin that preserves his core personality, his teaching role, his primary narrative functions, and the key dramatic beats of his arc (PoA, Shrieking Shack, DH confrontation, death). David Thewlis's performance captures his warmth, restraint, dry wit, and quiet authority with considerable accuracy. The main losses are in depth and texture rather than in fundamental characterization: the Greyback backstory (which contextualises his condition as deliberate harm rather than misfortune), the werewolf spy mission arc (which gives him moral complexity and self-awareness absent from the films), his explicit self-diagnosis as a habitual rationalizer of cowardice, his sharpest moral interventions (the Expelliarmus challenge, the Pensieve self-criticism), and the Teddy birth scene (the emotional resolution of his arc before death). These losses do not make him unrecognizable, but they remove the material that makes him genuinely complicated — a man who is admirable, self-aware, and persistently unable to overcome his deepest flaw. The result is a Lupin who is warmer and more straightforwardly sympathetic in the films than in the books, where his cowardice and self-sabotage are more consistently foregrounded.
